seo.title: Korean alphabet for beginners: first consonants ㄱ ㄴ ㅁ ㅅ ㅇ
seo.desc: Start reading Korean: the first five Hangul consonants and why each is shaped like your mouth. Free lesson with a quiz and typing practice.

blocks.md: Most alphabets grew slowly over centuries. **Hangul did not.** It was designed in the 1440s, by a committee, with a written explanation of *why* each letter looks the way it does.
That is the good news for you: the shapes are not random. Once you see the logic, five letters take about two minutes.
Each one is a picture of **what your mouth does** when you say it.

items.tip: The back of your tongue rising to the roof of your mouth. Say “g” and feel it.
The tip of your tongue touching just behind your teeth.
A mouth, closed. Square.
A tooth. Air hissing past it.
An open throat. At the start of a syllable it is silent, a placeholder.

blocks.md: **ㅇ is the strange one.** Korean syllables must start with a consonant, so when a syllable really starts with a vowel sound, ㅇ sits there holding the space and makes no sound at all.

blocks.q: Which letter is shaped like a closed mouth?
blocks.why: ㅁ is a square: a mouth closing for “m”.

blocks.q: You see 아 at the start of a word. What sound does ㅇ make here?
blocks.why: At the start of a syllable ㅇ is silent. It is only there so the vowel is not alone. (At the *bottom* it does make an “ng” sound, later.)

blocks.q: Type the letter for “n”.
blocks.why: ㄴ: tongue tip behind the teeth.

seo.title: Korean vowels ㅏ ㅓ ㅗ ㅜ ㅡ ㅣ: Hangul vowel practice
seo.desc: The six basic Korean vowels, built from a long line and a short mark. Free Hangul lesson: how each vowel sounds, plus a quiz and typing practice.

blocks.md: Vowels are built from three pieces: a **long line**, and a **short mark** that can sit on either side of it.
A vertical line means the short mark goes left or right. A horizontal line means it goes above or below. That is the whole system.

items.tip: as in f**a**ther. Mark on the right.
as in d**u**ll / b**u**t. Mark on the left.
as in b**o**at. Mark on top.
as in b**oo**t. Mark below.
No English match. Lips flat and wide, like the last sound in “open” said with a straight mouth.
as in mach**i**ne.

blocks.md: **ㅓ trips up English speakers.** It is *not* “eo” as two sounds. It is one vowel, close to the “u” in **but**. Written “eo” only because the Roman alphabet ran out of letters.

blocks.q: Which vowel sounds closest to the “u” in “but”?
blocks.why: ㅓ. The mark points left; the sound is that flat “uh”.

blocks.q: ㅗ and ㅜ look almost the same. What tells them apart?
options: The short mark is above for ㅗ, below for ㅜ
ㅜ is written twice as thick
blocks.why: Above = ㅗ (o). Below = ㅜ (u). Same idea as left/right on the vertical line.

blocks.q: Type the vowel that sounds like the “ee” in “machine”.

seo.title: How Hangul syllable blocks work (가, 고) / reading practice
seo.desc: Why Korean stacks letters into blocks, and where the consonant goes. Free Hangul lesson with listening, matching and a quiz.

blocks.md: Here is the part that makes Korean look hard and is actually the part that makes it easy.
Korean does not write letters in a line. It **stacks each syllable into a square block**. One block = one syllable, always.

blocks.h: The rule for where things go
blocks.md: It depends on the vowel:
That is why 가 and 고 use the same consonant but look so different. The letter did not change, the *shelf* did.

blocks.q: Listen. Which block did you hear?
Listen again.
You want to write “mu”. ㅁ is the consonant, ㅜ is the vowel. Where does ㅁ go?
blocks.why: ㅜ is a horizontal vowel, so the consonant sits on top: 무.

blocks.q: Match each block to its sound.

seo.title: Korean consonants ㄷ ㄹ ㅂ ㅈ ㅎ: how to say ㄹ
seo.desc: Five more Hangul consonants, and how to say ㄹ (between r and l). Free lesson with listening, a quiz, typing and your first Korean word.

blocks.md: You now have enough to read a lot. Five more and you have almost the whole set.

items.tip: ㄴ with a lid. Same tongue position, harder push.
Between English r and l. Tap the roof of your mouth once, like the “tt” in American “butter”.
ㅁ with the top opened.
ㅅ with a lid.
A lid, a line, and an open throat (ㅇ).

blocks.md: **Why “g / k”, “d / t”, “b / p”?** Korean does not hear these as two different letters. The same letter sounds softer between vowels and harder at the start. Native speakers do not notice the difference, you will not have to choose.

blocks.h: ㄹ is the one to practise
blocks.md: It is not the English r, and not quite the English l. Say **“butter”** the American way and freeze on that middle tap. That is ㄹ.

blocks.q: Listen.
ㄴ and ㄷ are related. How?
options: ㄷ is ㄴ with a line on top: same tongue position, stronger
ㄷ is only used at the end of words
They are unrelated; the shapes are coincidence
blocks.why: Adding a stroke means “same place in the mouth, more force”. That pattern runs through the whole alphabet.

blocks.q: Type the letter for the “h” sound.
Read it out loud. Your first real Korean word.

title.en: Adding a stroke, adding a y

seo.title: Korean y-vowels ㅑ ㅕ ㅛ ㅠ and ㅐ ㅔ
seo.desc: Double the mark, add a y: ㅑ ㅕ ㅛ ㅠ, plus ㅐ and ㅔ. Free Hangul lesson with listening and matching practice.

blocks.md: Remember the short mark on each vowel? **Double the mark and you add a “y” in front.** No new shapes to memorise.
These are not part of the pattern, just learn them.

items.tip: as in c**a**t.
as in b**e**d.

blocks.md: **ㅐ and ㅔ sound the same to most Koreans today.** They were different centuries ago. You do not need to hear a difference, you only need to spell them right, and that comes with words, not rules.

blocks.q: You know ㅗ is “o”. What is ㅛ?
Listen.
Match.

seo.title: Korean compound vowels ㅘ ㅝ ㅢ ㅟ ㅚ, two vowels together
seo.desc: Two vowels written as one: ㅘ ㅙ ㅚ ㅝ ㅞ ㅟ ㅢ, how they sound and where the consonant sits. Free Hangul practice with listening, typing and real words.

blocks.md: You know ㅗ and ㅏ. Put them together and you get **ㅘ, “wa”**. Korean builds its last vowels this way: **two vowels you already know, said fast, written as one**.
**One pattern to remember:** ㅗ teams up with ㅏ, and ㅜ teams up with ㅓ. You will never see ㅗ + ㅓ. The first vowel becomes a quick “w”, the second one is the vowel you hold.
These vowels have a flat part **and** a tall part, so the consonant sits in the **top-left corner** and the vowel wraps around it: ㄱ + ㅘ = 과, ㅁ + ㅝ = 뭐.

items.tip: ㄱ + ㅘ. As in 사과, apple.
ㅁ + ㅝ. “What?”: you will hear it all day.
ㅎ + ㅘ. As in 화장실, restroom.
ㄱ + ㅟ. Ear.
ㅇ + ㅢ. As in 의자, chair.

blocks.md: **ㅙ, ㅚ and ㅞ sound almost the same** in everyday Seoul speech, all close to “we” in **we**t. Like ㅐ and ㅔ, you learn which one to write with each word.
At the start of a word it is **ㅡ sliding into ㅣ**: 의사 (ui-sa, doctor). After a consonant it is said like ㅣ: 희망 sounds like “hi-mang”. You will meet the rest with real words.

blocks.q: Listen. Which one?
Listen again.
ㅗ + ㅏ make ㅘ. Which two make ㅝ?
blocks.why: ㅜ + ㅓ. ㅗ goes with ㅏ, ㅜ goes with ㅓ.

blocks.q: Type the block “gwa”: the second half of 사과, apple.
blocks.why: ㄱ in the corner, ㅘ wrapped around it.

blocks.q: Match.
The most useful sentence in any new country. Read it out loud.

seo.title: Korean double consonants ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ, aspirated vs tense
seo.desc: Hear the difference between 가, 카 and 까. Free Hangul lesson on aspirated (ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ ㅊ) and tense double consonants (ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ) with listening practice.

blocks.md: Korean splits consonants three ways where English has two. This is the one place English speakers need real practice.

Hold a slip of paper in front of your mouth.

**Aspirated (ㅋㅌㅍㅊ)**, the paper jumps. Big puff.

**Tense (ㄲㄸㅃㅆㅉ)**, the paper does not move at all. Throat tight, sound clipped.
Notice the writing follows the sound: **add a stroke** for aspirated, **write it twice** for tense. You are not memorising ten new letters, you are memorising two rules.

blocks.q: Listen. Plain or aspirated?
Listen.
ㅃ is written as two ㅂ. What does doubling mean?
options: Tense: tight throat, no puff of air

blocks.q: Both kinds in one word. Read it out loud.

seo.title: Korean batchim (final consonants) / the 7 ending sounds
seo.desc: The letter underneath a Korean block: any consonant can sit there, but only seven sounds come out. Free Hangul batchim lesson with listening and typing.

blocks.md: So far every block has been consonant + vowel. But a syllable can end in a consonant too, and it goes **underneath**. Korean calls it 받침 (*batchim*) / “the support”.

items.tip: ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ. The ㄴ sits under.
ㄱ + ㅜ + ㄱ.
ㅁ + ㅏ + ㄹ.

blocks.md: Any consonant can sit down there, but when it does, it collapses into **only seven sounds**.

head: Written at the bottom
Actually sounds like
rows: ㄷ ㅌ ㅅ ㅆ ㅈ ㅊ ㅎ

blocks.md: **“Unreleased” means you stop the sound and hold it.** English “cat” lets the t out. Korean 갓 does not, the tongue arrives and stays. This one habit makes an accent sound much more natural.

blocks.q: Remember ㅇ was silent at the start of a block. What about at the bottom?
options: It cannot go at the bottom
blocks.why: Top or side = silent placeholder. Bottom = “ng”. Same letter, two jobs.

blocks.q: Listen for the ending.
Type the block “han”: ㅎ, ㅏ, and ㄴ underneath.
blocks.why: ㅎ on the left, ㅏ on the right, ㄴ underneath.

seo.title: Korean linking sounds (연음) / how batchim moves to the next syllable
seo.desc: Why 한국어 is said han-gu-geo: a final consonant slides into the next silent ㅇ. Free Hangul reading lesson with listening and speaking practice.

blocks.md: One last thing and you can read anything. When a block ends in a consonant and the **next block starts with ㅇ** (the silent placeholder), that consonant slides over into the empty seat.
Nothing is spelled wrong. Korean **spells the meaning and speaks the flow**, the same way English writes “want to” and says “wanna”.

blocks.q: 한국어 is written 한 + 국 + 어. Why is it said “han-gu-geo”?
options: It is an exception you must memorise
The ㄱ under 국 slides into the empty ㅇ of 어
Koreans drop the ㄴ in fast speech
The spelling is old and the pronunciation changed

blocks.q: Listen. How many syllables do you hear?
Say it the way it sounds, not the way it is spelled.

seo.title: Read real Korean words: Hangul reading practice with loanwords
seo.desc: Put the whole alphabet to work: read coffee, taxi, computer and more in Korean. Free Hangul reading practice with matching and speaking.

blocks.md: No new letters. Everything below uses only what you already know, and these are words you will actually meet on your first day in Korea.
Korean borrowed a lot of words. Once you can read, **hundreds of words are free**, you already know what they mean.

blocks.q: You see 아이스크림 on a menu. What is it?
blocks.why: a-i-seu-keu-rim. Read it slowly and it says itself.

blocks.q: A sign says 화장실. It is somewhere you will need. Type what the first block is.
Match the loanword to its meaning.
The one everybody knows. You can now read it letter by letter.

seo.title: Hangul reading test: can you read Korean now?
seo.desc: A short test of the whole Korean alphabet: blocks, batchim and linking sounds. Free, no sign-up, listen, choose and read out loud.

blocks.md: A short test with no new material. If you get through this, you can read Korean out loud, and that was supposed to take months.

blocks.q: Listen, then pick the spelling.
Which of these ends in an “ng” sound?
맛있어요 is said “ma-si-sseo-yo”. Why does the ㅅ move?
options: It does not: that is a typo
The batchim slides into the next block’s empty ㅇ
ㅅ is always silent at the end

blocks.q: Put the letters in the right order to build 밥 (“rice”).
Last one. Match.
“I can read Korean.” Say it: it is true now.
